title: The data engineering lifecycle
summary: Data moves through generation, ingestion, storage, transformation and serving, supported by undercurrents that decide whether the platform can be trusted.

blocks.text: 2.1 The five stages

A widely used framing (popularized by Reis and Housley in *Fundamentals of Data Engineering*) describes every data platform as the same lifecycle: data is **generated** in source systems, **ingested** into the platform, **stored**, **transformed** into useful shapes and **served** to consumers. Tools change every few years; the stages do not.

blocks.title: The data engineering lifecycle
blocks.caption: Storage underpins every stage; data is stored at several points, not only once.

blocks.text: Each stage has its own failure modes. When a dashboard is wrong, walking the lifecycle backwards is a systematic way to find where the defect entered.
2.2 Generation and ingestion

**Generation** happens outside the data team's control: an OLTP database behind an application, a SaaS tool such as a CRM, IoT devices, clickstream trackers, files dropped by partners. The data team rarely owns these systems, so the key questions are about the relationship: who owns the source, how often its schema changes, whether it can tolerate extraction load, and whether changes will be announced.
**Ingestion** moves data from sources into the platform. It is usually the most fragile stage because it crosses an ownership boundary. The main patterns, covered in depth in chapters 16-20:

head: Pattern
How it works
Typical latency
Watch out for
rows: Copy the whole table on a schedule
Cost grows with table size; misses deletes only if you diff
Log retention, schema changes, operational setup
Producers publish events to a log such as Kafka
Poll vendor APIs, often via a managed tool
Rate limits, pagination, vendor schema changes

blocks.text: Incremental loads keyed on `updated_at` silently miss rows when the application updates data without touching that column, or when rows are hard-deleted. If correctness matters, use CDC or a periodic full reconciliation.
2.3 Storage, transformation and serving

**Storage** is not a stage you pass through once. Raw data is stored on landing, again after cleaning, again as modelled tables and sometimes again in a serving cache. Choices here (object storage versus warehouse-managed storage, file format, table format, retention) shape cost and flexibility for years; see chapters 3, 4 and 21.

**Transformation** turns raw records into something consumers can use: type casting, deduplication, conforming keys across sources, joining, applying business rules, building dimensional models and aggregates. Transformations are where business logic lives, which makes them the part that most needs version control, testing and review.

**Serving** delivers data to its consumers. Analysts and BI tools query modelled tables, ideally through a semantic layer (chapter 35). Data scientists read feature tables. **Reverse ETL** pushes modelled data back into operational tools, for example customer scores into a CRM. Applications may query a low-latency OLAP store through an API (chapter 46). Each serving path implies different latency, concurrency and access-control needs.

blocks.title: Tracing a wrong revenue number
blocks.text: Finance reports that yesterday's revenue on the dashboard is 4% lower than the billing system. The platform team walks the lifecycle backwards.
items: Serving: the dashboard query filters on a status list that is up to date.
Transformation: the revenue model joins orders to payments with an inner join.
Storage: the payments table is missing rows for a two-hour window.
Ingestion: the incremental job's watermark advanced past rows committed late by a long-running transaction.
Fix: overlap the incremental window (re-read the last N minutes) and deduplicate on the primary key.

blocks.text: 2.4 The undercurrents
Beneath the stages run cross-cutting concerns that apply everywhere. Platforms that ignore them work in a demo and then decay.

layers.label: Software engineering
layers.sub: version control, code review, modular code

items: **Security**: least-privilege access, encryption in transit and at rest, secrets kept out of code, audit logs. Ingestion credentials into production databases are a prime target.
**Data management**: governance, metadata and catalogs, lineage, data quality, master data, retention and deletion. It answers *what is this table, who owns it and can I trust it*.
**DataOps**: applying DevOps practice to data: automated tests on data and code, CI/CD for pipelines, monitoring of freshness and volume, incident handling with runbooks.

**Orchestration**: coordinating jobs with dependencies, schedules or event triggers, retries and backfills (chapter 30). Not the same as scheduling: a cron table knows times, an orchestrator knows dependencies.
**Software engineering**: pipelines are software. They need version control, review, modular design, tests and reproducible environments.

blocks.text: Use the undercurrents as a review checklist for any proposed architecture. Gaps here are more common than gaps in the main data path.
2.5 ETL versus ELT

**ETL** (extract, transform, load) transforms data in a separate engine before loading it into the warehouse. It dominated when warehouse compute was expensive and fixed in size: you did not want raw, messy data taking up warehouse capacity. **ELT** (extract, load, transform) loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse or lakehouse with SQL. It became the default once cloud warehouses offered elastic compute and cheap storage.

head: Aspect
ETL
ELT
rows: Often not; only transformed output lands
Yes, raw is loaded and kept, enabling replays
Managed loaders plus dbt or SQLMesh
Sensitive data can be masked before landing; less warehouse compute
Simple loaders, replayable history, SQL-first teams
Raw PII lands in the warehouse; compute costs can grow unchecked

blocks.title: ELT step: deduplicate raw CDC rows into a clean table (Snowflake)
blocks.text:
create or replace table silver.customers as
select
    id            as customer_id,
    lower(email)  as email,
    country_code,
    updated_at
from raw.app_customers
qualify row_number() over (
    partition by id
    order by updated_at desc
) = 1;

Most modern platforms are hybrid: light transformations in flight (masking PII, flattening payloads), heavy business logic in the warehouse or lakehouse. The useful question is *where does each transformation run best, given cost, latency and governance?*

ELT does not mean *load everything and sort it out later*. Without a layered design (chapter 12), contracts and ownership, an ELT warehouse becomes a swamp of near-duplicate tables nobody dares delete.
2.6 Using the lifecycle as a design tool

When designing a new pipeline or platform, write one line per stage plus one per undercurrent. It forces decisions that otherwise get deferred: late data, where PII is masked, who is paged, how a backfill runs.

blocks.title: Lifecycle sheet for a subscription business
blocks.text: A subscription company wants churn analytics from its Postgres application database, Stripe billing data and a product analytics event stream. Fill in a lifecycle sheet: for each of the five stages and five undercurrents, write the concrete choice and the main risk. Identify the stage you expect to cause the most incidents and explain why.
hints: Consider who owns each source and how its schema changes are announced.
Decide where PII such as email addresses is masked or tokenized.

items: The lifecycle is generation, ingestion, storage, transformation and serving; storage recurs at several points.
Ingestion is the most fragile stage because it crosses an ownership boundary.
Undercurrents (security, data management, DataOps, orchestration, software engineering) separate a demo from a platform.
ELT loads raw data and transforms in the warehouse; ETL transforms before loading. Most platforms are hybrid.
Walking the lifecycle backwards is a systematic way to locate a data defect.

blocks.q: Why did ELT largely replace ETL as the default for cloud analytics?
options: Elastic warehouse compute and cheap storage made loading raw data first practical
SQL became faster than other languages
ELT removes the need for data modelling
ETL tools stopped supporting cloud sources
blocks.explain: Separated, elastic compute and cheap storage made it affordable to load raw data and transform it in place. ELT still needs modelling; it only moves where transformation runs.

blocks.q: An incremental load filters on `updated_at > last_watermark`. Which problem can it NOT detect on its own?
options: Rows with a NULL in a non-key column
New rows inserted after the last run
blocks.explain: A deleted row no longer exists to be selected, so the filter never sees it. Inserts and properly stamped updates are exactly what the filter captures.

blocks.q: What distinguishes an orchestrator from a plain scheduler such as cron?
options: Schedulers cannot run jobs at night
Orchestrators model dependencies between tasks, plus retries and backfills
blocks.explain: Cron triggers at times; an orchestrator knows that task B depends on task A and handles retries, state and backfills. Many orchestrators also use time schedules, so being event-driven is not the distinction.

blocks.q: Which is a legitimate reason to transform data before it lands in the warehouse?
options: Raw data cannot be stored in object storage
Sensitive fields must be masked or tokenized before they reach a broadly accessible store
blocks.explain: Masking PII in flight keeps it out of the analytical store entirely, a governance benefit of ETL-style steps. The other statements are false for modern warehouses.
